title: Shared proteomic signature between a rat model of hypertension and Alzheimer’s disease point to cerebrovascular changes in extracellular vesicles
projectDescription: Untreated hypertension is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, this association is not well understood, mainly due to the lack of animal models. The aim of this study was to reveal novel proteins and pathways that underlie AD associated with hypertension. Using untargeted proteomics, we analyzed brain samples from the frontal cortex of human AD (Braak stages 4-6), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), non-demented controls (Braak stages 0-3), aged (30 and 40 week-old) hypertensive rats, and age-matched normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY) controls. We identified 199 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) when comparing 40-week-old SHRs to age-matched WKY control rats. Moreover, our analysis of human samples identify more than 1300 DEPs in AD when compared to control. Using a cross-species comparison, we identify 24 candidate proteins in the SHR model, whose trajectory pattern over hypertension progression align with those observed in the AD Braak staging progression. The identified candidate proteins associate significantly with the “Extracellular exosomes” pathway and are dysregulated around the cerebrovasculature in both SHR and AD brains. Our findings demonstrate cross-species translatability between AD and the SHR, and provide novel mechanistic insights into a shared dysregulation of extracellular vesicles.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Tissues (approximately 0.3 cm × 0.3 cm × 0.3 cm) were homogenized in 300 μl of ice-cold lysis buffer (50 mM Tris pH 8.5; 5 mM EDTA pH 8.0; 150 mM NaCl; 10 mM KCl; 1% NP-40; and 1X complete protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, cat no. 04693124001)) by three rounds of chopping the tissue using dissection scissors and a handheld homogenizer. The homogenates were centrifuged at 11,000g for 10 min at 4 °C to obtain the supernatant. Protein quantification of the tissue extracts was determined by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat no. 23227). Tissue extracts (50 μg protein) were diluted in digestion buffer containing 0.5% sodium deoxycholate in 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate and heated to 70 °C for 10 min. The samples were then cooled on ice and prepared using filter-aided sample preparation (FASP)  with flat spin filters (Microcon-10 kDa, Cat no. MRCPRT010). The samples were reduced and alkylated in digestion buffer containing 1:50 (v:v) tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (0.5 M, Sigma) and 1:10 (v:v) 2-chloroacetamide (0.5 M, Sigma) for 30 min at 37 C. Proteolytic digestion was performed overnight at 37 °C by addition of 0.5 μg Trypsin/LysC mix (Promega, cat no. V5072) (at enzyme to protein ratio 1:100). Centrifugation at 14,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C was employed between the different steps. The resulting peptides were desalted using stage-tips containing a Poly-styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer modified with sulfonic acid groups (SDB-RPS; 3M) material, as previously described. The eluted peptide mixture was dried down using SpeedVac vacuum centrifugation and stored at -80 °C until further analysis.   Peptide mixtures (1 and 5 µl injections of rat and human samples, respectively) were analyzed on Bruker timsTOF mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) using positive ion mode, with a Captivespray ion source on-line connected to a Dionex Ultimate 3000RSnano chromatography system (Thermo Fisher). Peptides were separated on an Aurora column with captive spray insert (C18 1.6 uM particles, 15 cm, 75 μm inner diameter; IonOptics) at 60 °C. A solvent gradient of buffer A (0.1 % formic acid) and buffer B (99.9 % acetonitrile/0.1 % formic acid) was used over 22 min for human samples and 28 min for rat samples, at a flow rate of 400 nL/min and 600 nL/min for human and rat samples, respectively. The mass spectrometer was operated in DIA PASEF mode with 1.1 s cycle time and TIMS ramp time of 100.0 ms. MS scan range was set to 100–1700 m/z.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw DIA files were analyzed with DIA-NN software (v.1.8.1) separately (https://github.com/vdemichev/diann). An in silico DIA-NN predicted spectral library was generated using UniProt FASTA databases for Rattus norvegicus; (UP000002494_10116.fasta and UP000002494_10116_additional.fasta, downloaded August 2020), and for Homo sapiens; (UP000005640_9606 and UP000005640_9606_additional, downloaded April 2022). The DIA-NN search included the following settings: ‘FASTA digest for library-free search/library generation’ and ‘Deep learning-based spectra, RTs, and IMs prediction’ were enabled, Digestion protease = Trypsin/P; missed cleavage = 1; max number of variable modifications = 1; methionine oxidation (UniMod:35) was considered as variable modification; N-term M excision = True; C carbamidomethylation = True; peptide length range = 7 to 30; precursor charge range = 1 to 4; precursor m/z range = 300 to 1800; fragment ion m/z range = 200 to 1800; Precursor false discovery rate (FDR) (%) = 1%; Use isotopologs = enabled; MBR = enabled; Neural network classifier = single-pass mode; Protein inference = Genes; Quantification strategy = Any LC (high accuracy); Cross-run normalization = RT-dependent; Library generation = Smart profiling; Speed and RAM usage = Optimal results.
